newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Right-wingers sought in South African bombing.
newsitem.headline: Right-wingers sought in South African bombing.

text.p: South African police said on Thursday they were hunting three fugitive right-wingers in connection with a Christmas Eve bomb attack that killed four people in a small farming town.

Spokesman John Sterrenberg said the three whites had already been convicted of murder in absentia for planting bombs that killed 20 people on the eve of South Africa's historic all-race election in April 1994.
The men were among four members of the neo-Nazi Afrikaner Resistance Movement (AWB) who escaped from custody in March last year, weeks before their convictions were handed down.
A total of nine AWB members were sentenced to 26 years in jail each for the election bombs which went off in and around Johannesburg and its international airport.

Sterrenberg said Abraham Myburgh, Jan de Wet and Nicolaas Barnard "could possibly be of assistance" in the investigation into the twin pipe bombs which exploded on December 24 in Worcester, 90 km (55 miles) northeast of Cape Town.

An adult and three children were killed and about 60 people were wounded by the blasts at a supermarket and pharmacy crowded with Christmas shoppers. Most of the casualties were blacks or people of mixed-race descent, known in South Africa as coloureds.
Sterrenberg said forensic tests in the Worcester bombing were nearly finished but no details could be disclosed.
Police said immediately after the attack that they were looking for three men seen fleeing the area. They offered a reward of half a million rand ($107,000).
Police Minister Sydney Mufamadi and Justice Minister Dullah Omar have both suggested right-wingers opposed to black majority rule could be responsible for the Worcester bombing.

"As far as these people continuing on the course of violence and destruction are concerned, they need to know they have stretched our patience to the limit," Mufamadi said the day after the attack. "They will pay the price for failing to reciprocate our commitment to reconciliation."

Days before the Worcester blasts President Nelson Mandela extended the cut-off date for political crimes to be eligible for amnesty under legislation setting up the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

The date was originally set as December 1993, which would have excluded the right-wing election bombers, but Mandela extended it at the urging of commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu. The cut-off is now May 10, 1994, the date of Mandela's inauguration.

Hardline right-wingers like AWB leader Eugene Terre Blanche issued frequent warnings of civil war ahead of the 1994 election, demanding self-rule for Afrikaners, but their potential to cause serious disruption had appeared to dissipate in the last three years.
